newsitem.title: FRANCE: FRANCE'S PICARDIE WHEAT AREA SEES 10 PCT YIELD CUT.
newsitem.headline: FRANCE'S PICARDIE WHEAT AREA SEES 10 PCT YIELD CUT.

text.p: France's second biggest soft wheat region, Picardie, in the northeast of the country, expects to see a 10 percent drop in yields from last year's abnormally high nine tonnes per hectare, local crop officials said on Tuesday.
Harvesting was held up for several days by last week's storms which flattened a handful of grain fields in the region's south.
But the harvest is now back in full swing and should be finished this week, crop experts said.
"Yields are lower than last year by about 10 percent," a crop official at the regional capital of Amiens said.
The weather service warned of potential new storms in the north of Picardie near Belgium on Wednesday.

Picardie is one of the northern French regions that pulled off remarkable increases in yields after perfect late-harvest weather in 1996. Its local yield was 35 percent above the French average in a record wheat year.
However, experts said this year's yields in the flat, exposed region varied in a wide range from six to 10 tonnes per hectare for an average 10 percent decline.
Using the most recently published regional area estimate of 508,000 hectares, a 10-percent lower yield of 8.1 tonnes a hectare implies output of 4.11 million tonnes, down six percent from 1996.
The farm ministry earlier predicted a yield decrease of 0.7 tonnes in Picardie but did not say what figure it was using as a base.
Moisture has also been driving down test weight in early samples but there are few precise figures.
Local officials had no confirmation so far on reports of pre-germination caused by the wet.
The region's barley harvest is finished. Locally, yields are seen down slightly to 7.6 tonnes a hectare from 7.8 or 7.9 tonnes, officials said.
That implies a slight rise in output to 885,000 tonnes due to a three percent rise in area.
But within this total local analysts saw a mixed bag of quality, with a greater proportion of the barley crop seen too high in protein to make it for malting.
"There are some protein problems and poor calibration (too many small grains) for the Plaisant variety," one analyst said.
In the Somme, which is Picardie's main barley growing area, early tests showed that 50 or 60 percent of the crop was coming in as malting compared with 75 or 80 percent in a normal year.
